territorial_scope.description: Applies to persons engaged in commerce, with those terms defined by reference to the Fair Labor Standards Act; no extraterritorial reach is stated.

evidence.quote: The terms “commerce” and “person” have the meanings given the terms in section 3 of the Fair Labor Standards Act of 1938 (29 U.S.C. 203).

summary.short: Bars persons from surveillance-based price setting and surveillance-based wage setting using automated decision systems, subject to exceptions for price setting. Requires publishing accuracy and correction procedures 180 days before use. Enforced by the FTC, state attorneys general and private suits.
summary.long: Introduced bill that would prohibit a person from engaging in surveillance-based price setting: using an automated decision system to offer or inform a customized price based in whole or part on surveillance data, subject to exceptions for cost-based differences, broadly defined group discounts and affirmatively enrolled loyalty programs with conditions. It would prohibit surveillance-based wage setting, except where the system uses only data on the worker's city or state and its cost of living. Persons using such systems for price or wage setting must publish, at least 180 days in advance, procedures on data accuracy, correction and disclosure. Violations are treated as FTC rule violations; state attorneys general may sue for injunctions and the greater of actual damages or $3,000 per violation; the EEOC may sue for wage violations; injured persons have a private right of action, with awards of up to three times the amount for willful violations, fee-shifting, a five-year limitation period, and pre-dispute arbitration agreements and joint action waivers made unenforceable for such claims. The Act preempts only directly conflicting state laws and preserves collective bargaining, where employers must give advance notice and a bargaining opportunity before using such systems to set compensation.

relations.target_text: Federal Trade Commission Act (15 U.S.C. 41 et seq.)
relations.note: Applies the FTC Act's jurisdiction, powers and penalties to enforcement of Sec. 2(a) and its regulations, and to Sec. 3 via Sec. 3(d). Also cross-references FTC Act sections 18(a)(1)(B), 4, 5(a)(2) and 6 (15 U.S.C. 57a(a)(1)(B), 44, 45(a), 46) and 15 U.S.C. 45(a) for unfair methods of competition.

relations.target_text: Communications Act of 1934 (47 U.S.C. 151 et seq.)
relations.note: Extends FTC enforcement of Sec. 2(a) to common carriers subject to the Communications Act of 1934, notwithstanding the FTC's jurisdictional limits.

relations.target_text: Federal Arbitration Act (chapter 1 of title 9, United States Code)
relations.note: Provides that a pre-dispute arbitration agreement or joint action waiver is not valid or enforceable for purposes of the private right of action, notwithstanding the Federal Arbitration Act. The same clause appears in Sec. 3(f)(6).

evidence.quote: Notwithstanding chapter 1 of title 9, United States Code (commonly known as the “Federal Arbitration Act”)

notes: Bill text as introduced (legislative_stage: introduced). No legal_basis, amends, repeals, implements or enacted_by_bill relations are stated. Target statutes are cited by U.S. Code reference and are not in the registry, so target_instrument_id is an empty string. Internal issues: Sec. 3(c) first names the 'Equal Opportunity Commission' and then the 'Equal Employment Opportunity Commission'; Sec. 3(f)(2) refers to 'subparagraph (A)(ii)', which does not exist in Sec. 3(f)(1) (the $3,000 amount is in (B)(ii)); Sec. 2(e)(1) and Sec. 3(g)(1) define 'automated decision system' differently; Sec. 5(a) refers to 'surveillance-based wage discrimination', a term the bill does not define (Sec. 3 defines 'surveillance-based wage setting').

thresholds.note: No numeric cutoff changes scope, eligibility, exemption, obligation tier, prohibition, benefit tier or price tier. The only dollar figure is the $3,000 statutory damages amount in Sec. 2(c)(1)(C)(ii), 2(d)(1)(B)(ii), 3(e)(3)(B) and 3(f)(1)(B)(ii), which is a per-violation remedy amount and is treated as enforcement under the codebook, not as a threshold. The 180-day publication periods in Sec. 2(a)(3) and 3(b) are procedural time limits (events), and the 3-times multiplier for willful violations and the 5-year limitation period are enforcement and procedural terms.
